lead: Every heat transfer carries a hidden tax. A reservoir at T delivers heat Q, but the surroundings sit at T₀. Only part of Q can become work; the rest must be dumped as heat to the surroundings, however good the engine. This chapter defines the dead state, splits Q into available and unavailable energy, and extends the split to a closed system. Power plants, data-centre cooling and solar thermal design use this split to judge how much work is really on offer.
prereq: You need entropy and reversible processes from Unit 3, Entropy, and the closed-system first law from Unit 2, First Law.

blocks.text: The dead state is the state of the surroundings: temperature T₀ and pressure p₀. At this state a system has no unused potential to produce work. Choose T₀ and p₀ once for a problem and keep them fixed. All availability in this chapter is measured relative to that state.
A source at absolute temperature T gives heat Q. The best engine between T and T₀ is reversible. Its Carnot efficiency is 1 − T₀/T, so the largest work is:

blocks.where: A is available energy in kJ; Q is heat supplied in kJ; T is source absolute temperature in K; T₀ is dead-state temperature in K; ΔS = Q/T is entropy delivered by the source in kJ/K.

blocks.text: The remaining heat cannot become work. It must go to the surroundings. The source loses entropy ΔS = Q/T. At T₀ that entropy carries heat T₀ΔS. Thus unavailable energy is T₀ΔS. Some syllabi call A availability and T₀ΔS anergy.
For a closed system, use internal energy U, volume V and entropy S. The dead state has U₀, V₀ and S₀ at T₀ and p₀. The non-flow availability is:
Φ = (U − U₀) + p₀(V − V₀) − T₀(S − S₀)
blocks.where: Φ is the maximum useful work as the system reaches the dead state, in kJ; U, V, S are system state values; U₀, V₀, S₀ are dead-state values; p₀ is dead-state pressure in kPa; T₀ is dead-state temperature in K.

blocks.text: The term U − U₀ is energy stored above the dead state. p₀(V − V₀) is work the surroundings do or absorb as volume changes. T₀(S − S₀) subtracts the part locked by entropy. Kinetic and potential terms are added separately when present. Flowing-stream exergy is in 4.2.

A property depends only on the state of the system. Φ depends also on T₀ and p₀, so it is not a property. Change the environment and the same system state has a different Φ. For the heat example, at T₀ = 300 K and T = 500 K the available fraction is 0.40. Raise T to 1000 K and it becomes 0.70.

items: At T = T₀ the available fraction is zero: no work from heat at environment temperature.
As T becomes large, 1 − T₀/T approaches one: hot heat is nearly all available.
Keep T and T₀ in kelvin in every formula.

figure.caption: The available fraction 1 − T₀/T rises with source temperature, while the unavailable fraction T₀/T falls; at 500 K the split is 0.40 and 0.60.

spec.aria: Two curves that add to one: the available fraction 1 − 300/T rises with source temperature while the unavailable fraction 300/T falls.

examples.question: Heat of 1000 kJ is supplied from a reservoir at 500 K. The environment is at 300 K. Find the available part, the unavailable part, and the entropy change of the reservoir. Check that the two parts add to Q.
steps: Given: Q = 1000 kJ, T = 500 K, T₀ = 300 K.
Entropy delivered by the reservoir: ΔS = Q/T = 1000/500 = 2 kJ/K.
examples.answer: Available energy is 400 kJ, unavailable energy is 600 kJ, and the reservoir entropy change is 2 kJ/K.
examples.check:
Q = 1000.0
T = 500.0
T0 = 300.0
A = Q * (1 - T0 / T)
dS = Q / T
U = T0 * dS
total = A + U
print(A)
print(dS)
print(U)
print(total)

traps: Putting °C into 1 − T₀/T. Convert both temperatures to kelvin first.
Using the sink or working-fluid temperature instead of T₀. T₀ is fixed by the environment.
Treating T₀ΔS as the heat an actual engine rejects. An irreversible engine rejects more; T₀ΔS is the reversible-limit unavailable part.
Calling availability a property. It changes when the dead state changes.
Using flow exergy in a closed-system question. Flow exergy belongs to 4.2.

quiz.a: The environment state at T₀ and p₀ at which the system has no potential to produce work.

quiz.q: Write unavailable energy in terms of Q, T₀ and T.
quiz.a: Unavailable energy = T₀ΔS = T₀Q/T, with T and T₀ in kelvin.

quiz.q: Why is unavailable energy T₀ΔS and not just Q/T?
quiz.a: ΔS = Q/T is entropy. Multiplying entropy by T₀ converts it to heat that must be dumped to the environment at T₀.

quiz.q: Heat of 600 kJ comes from a source at 600 K. The environment is at 300 K. Find the available energy and the unavailable energy.
Heat of 2000 kJ comes from a source at 800 K. The environment is at 300 K. Find the available energy.
Two sources at 500 K and 1000 K each deliver 1000 kJ to the same environment at 300 K. Compare their available energies.
quiz.a: At 500 K, A = 1000(1 − 300/500) = 400 kJ. At 1000 K, A = 1000(1 − 300/1000) = 700 kJ. The hotter source gives 300 kJ more available energy.

quiz.q: Why does availability depend on T₀ and p₀ while U, V and S do not?
quiz.a: U, V and S are properties fixed by the system state. Availability is the maximum work relative to a chosen environment, so changing T₀ or p₀ changes it.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, exergy analysis sizes heat recovery, district heating and data-centre cooling; anergy is the part that must be rejected. Researchers extend the idea to chemical exergy and life-cycle accounting. Search next: exergy, anergy, dead state, exergy destruction, second-law efficiency.
